name: Beer-Lambert law
seoDesc: Beer-Lambert law: work out concentration from the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance. A free chemistry calculator with the formula, units and…
summary: Supply the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance and the Beer-Lambert law calculator solves for concentration. That makes it useful for a bench calculation involving amounts, concentrations or reaction ratios. Nothing repaints underneath you: edit a field, press Calculate, and the new answer appears. That is how you find out which input the result is sensitive to.

sections.title: How does the Beer-Lambert law calculator work?
sections.html:
The Beer-Lambert law calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports concentration in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance.

Press Calculate once and the page holds the relationship, tracking which boxes you filled and working out everything else; from that point on it follows every edit you make.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: What do you need to enter?
sections.html:
• A measured quantity, entered by default in molars. The unit chip switches it to any of the 9 supported units.
  • A plain number with no unit attached.

sections.title: The formula behind the Beer-Lambert law calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Concentration=absorbance ÷ (molar absorption coefficient × path length)
Transmittance=100 × the exponential of (-absorbance × the natural log of (10))
Concentration=(-the natural log of (transmittance) + the natural log of (100)) ÷ (molar absorption coefficient × path length × the natural log of (10))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• Shown in moles, and convertible to any of the 5 units on that chip.
  • A number, filled in as soon as the inputs allow it.
  • Shown in centimeters, and convertible to any of the 34 units on that chip.

Before doubting the arithmetic, check the inputs: a unit chip on the wrong setting, a drop-down left at its default, or a percentage typed as a whole number rather than a decimal will each shift the answer by a clean power of ten.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Molar concentration, opening in molars
  • Mole, opening in moles
  • Length, opening in centimeters

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Beer-Lambert law calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Preparing a solution and checking the numbers first
  • Working through a stoichiometry problem
  • Converting between the units a protocol and your bench equipment use
  • Any time the same 2 figures keep coming back — the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Keep the units you enter consistent. Mixing centimetres into a field that expects metres is the single most common way to get an answer that is out by a factor of a hundred.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Fields that are still blank are exactly the ones the calculator has not yet been given, so the results panel is a reliable map of what is missing.

sections.title: What are the limits worth knowing?
sections.html:
Every tool draws a boundary somewhere. For the Beer-Lambert law calculator, these are the ones that matter:

  • The unit chips cover the units listed on the page. A historical or regional unit that is missing can still be used by converting it to a listed unit first.
  • The calculator reports what the relationship implies; it does not judge whether the inputs themselves are sensible, so a figure that is out by a factor of ten will produce an answer that is out by the same factor.

sections.title: How do you check the answer yourself?
sections.html:
• Change one input at a time — molar absorption coefficient for instance — and watch which results move. A result that stays put does not depend on it.
  • Try a round value you can work out in your head. If the answer matches your mental arithmetic, the inputs are on the scale you assumed.
  • Switch the units to the ones you normally use and confirm the numbers are unchanged apart from their label; if they are not, a chip was on the wrong setting.

faq.q: What does the Beer-Lambert law calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns concentration, derived from the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Beer-Lambert law calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the molar absorption coefficient and the absorbance, which is 2 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter molar absorption coefficient in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Molar absorption coefficient opens in molars and the chip beside it offers 9 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: Is the Beer-Lambert law calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — press Calculate and every result updates together.
